title: Losar, the fifth time
hookLine: the new year: clean, renew, begin
tomorrow: a full-moon verse has three lines. why is the third about the mind?

lines: A GLOWING STRANGER AT THE SPRING.
"THE VERSE OF THE ONE GOOD NIGHT?"
cards: New planners get bought, gyms fill up, and last year's resolution gets written down again, word for word.
Losar, the Tibetan new year, starts with a broom instead: in the last days of the old year, houses are scrubbed top to bottom. The suttas have a clean start of their own.
A monk named Samiddhi bathes in a hot spring before dawn and stands on the bank in one robe, drying off.
A being appears, so bright the whole spring glows, and asks him a question: do you know the verse of the one good night? He doesn't. Learn it, the being says, and vanishes.

teach.b: So Samiddhi goes to the Buddha and asks. The verse, in paraphrase: don't run after the past, don't build your hopes on the future. The past is left behind; the future hasn't come.
Whatever is here now, see it clearly, right where it is, unshaken. Someone who lives like that, day and night, has had one good night.

Then, the sutta says, the Buddha got up and went into his dwelling without explaining a word. The monks had to ask Mahakaccana, a disciple known for opening up short sayings. His answer is the surprise.

Running after the past, he says, isn't remembering. It's replaying what you once saw and heard with longing, and letting the mind be tied to it. Chasing the future is the same knot, tied to what hasn't happened.
So this isn't a teaching against memory. It's a teaching against clinging, in both directions. Set beside Losar, it gives the broom a second job.
In Tibetan homes, tradition says, the cleaning is a letting go: old dust and old troubles carried out the door, so the new year can start in a clean room.

teach.h: CARRY OUT THE CLINGING, KEEP THE PHOTOS.
teach.b: The point isn't to throw out the family photos; it's to carry out the clinging.
A fresh year, in this teaching, isn't a year with no past. It's a year where the past stops holding the broom.

how: Before Losar, Tibetan families clean their houses top to bottom and carry the old year's troubles out of the house; at the new year they make offerings at the home shrine, visit monasteries and family, and share food.

o: the Tibetan new year, begun by cleaning the house
a Tibetan day for honoring the dead with lamps
the Tibetan festival of the Buddha's first sermon

games.q: the one good night — tap the pairs.
p: bathing at a hot spring before dawn
asked about the one good night
the new year, begun with a broom

s: the one-good-night verse says to forget your past
Mahakaccana explains it as not clinging to the past with longing, not erasing memory.
the Buddha recited the verse and left without explaining it
he went into his dwelling, and the monks asked Mahakaccana.
Tibetan homes are cleaned top to bottom before Losar
the old year's dust and troubles are carried out before the new year starts.

games.q: your friend starts the new year by deleting every old photo so she can 'live in the now.' what would the one-good-night verse say?
o: the verse is about not clinging to the past, not deleting memories.
good move; the verse says cut every tie to the past right away.
first plan the future in detail; then the past can't hurt her.
games.why: Mahakaccana explained running after the past as replaying it with longing. seeing what's here clearly doesn't require erasing anything.

practice: Pick one small corner near you: a shelf, the edge of a desk, the top of a drawer. Clear it and wipe it slowly, and each time a thought of last year or next year pulls at you, bring your hand back to the surface it's on.
Then sit beside the clean spot, here, now.

wordCard.voice: Losar: the Tibetan new year, begun with a broom and a clean house, the old year's troubles carried out the door.

carryVoice: The line for the new year: a fresh year, with the past let go, not erased. Six of seven, swept.
